hook.text: A supercharger does the same job as a turbo but runs off the engine's crankshaft via a belt.

buildup.text: Because it's belt-driven, a supercharger delivers instant boost with zero lag at any speed.

discovery.text: Roots-type blowers sit on top of the engine and force air straight into the intake manifold.

twist.text: The trade-off is parasitic loss—the supercharger steals some engine power to create its boost.

climax.text: Dodge's Hellcat used a massive supercharged V8 to hit 707 horsepower from the factory.

punchline.text: Instant power comes at the cost of driving the blower.

quiz.question: How is a supercharger powered?
options: By a belt from the crankshaft

details.summary: Superchargers are belt-driven compressors that force extra air into the engine, providing instant power boost without the turbo lag of exhaust-driven turbochargers, at the cost of parasitic drag on the engine.
details.whyItMatters: Superchargers deliver immediate throttle response that turbochargers cannot match, making them preferred for applications where instant power delivery matters more than peak efficiency.
takeaways: They are driven mechanically by the engine's crankshaft via a belt
Power boost is immediate with no lag at any engine speed
They consume engine power to operate, reducing net efficiency gains

faq.question: Why are turbochargers more popular than superchargers today?
faq.answer: Turbochargers use waste exhaust energy, making them more efficient than belt-driven superchargers. As fuel economy regulations tightened, the efficiency advantage of turbocharging made it the preferred forced induction method.

faq.question: What types of superchargers exist?
faq.answer: Three main types: Roots, twin-screw, and centrifugal. Roots and twin-screw mount on top of the engine and provide strong low-RPM boost. Centrifugal units resemble turbochargers and are more efficient at high RPM.
